Phenotype-scope guard: the sleep-disordered breathing of diaphragm dysfunction is predominantly REM-related hypoventilation (ventilatory-pump failure), not classic obstructive apnea; the sleep-apnea catalog identity is broader, so PSG confirmation of the SDB phenotype and exclusion of an obesity-dominant obstructive phenotype are required for individual attribution.
Referred-population guard: both PSG cohorts studied patients referred for sleep evaluation, so the near-universal SDB findings cannot be read as population prevalence.
governanceNotes: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY with NOT_ESTABLISHED consensus and hypothesizedOnly mechanism despite quantified REM-SDB anchors (RDI 26.0 vs 0.7 controls): the quantified cohorts are small (n=11 instrumented; n=66 referred) with ascertainment bias, the SDB phenotype is REM-hypoventilation rather than the obstructive phenotype the target identity most often denotes, and no incident cohort establishes progression from stable unilateral dysfunction to clinically diagnosed sleep-apnea.
Bilateral-dysfunction severity gradient recorded: bilateral dysfunction carried 6.8-fold CPAP failure, so laterality/bilaterality documentation materially affects the pathway's clinical weight.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The instrumented PSG cohort found a REM respiratory disturbance index of 26.0 events/h in hemidiaphragm paralysis or severe weakness versus 0.7 in matched controls, with diaphragm EMG drive doubled and rising further in REM (Steier 2008); the Mayo referral cohort found significant sleep-disordered breathing (mean AHI 26.6) in all 66 patients with isolated diaphragmatic dysfunction, with CPAP controlling SDB in only 37.9% (Khan 2014); the perioperative review documents phrenic-nerve-output inhibition causing diaphragmatic dysfunction with post-surgical sleep-disordered breathing (Rock 2003).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the ventilatory-pump pathway is quantitatively anchored but both cohorts are sleep-laboratory-referred populations; the SDB phenotype is REM-related hypoventilation rather than the obstructive phenotype that dominates the target identity; no incident cohort tracks progression from stable dysfunction to diagnosed sleep-apnea; and obesity-related obstructive disease operates independently in the same patients.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized ventilatory-pump pathway: diaphragm paralysis removes the primary inspiratory muscle's contribution; during REM sleep the diaphragm is the only active inspiratory muscle and accessory-muscle tone falls, so the weakened hemidiaphragm paradoxically moves and alveolar ventilation drops; recurrent REM hypoventilation, desaturation, and arousals present as sleep-disordered breathing with an apnea-hypopnea pattern. Bilateral dysfunction amplifies the same pathway, which is why bilateral patients fail single-level CPAP support more often.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The REM-dependence of SDB in diaphragm dysfunction is physiologically well characterized and quantified in two cohorts, but referral ascertainment, the phenotype mismatch with the obstructive-dominant target identity, and the absence of an incidence denominator keep the mapping at association strength. Etiological consensus is NOT_ESTABLISHED and no nexus probability is asserted.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: transdiaphragmatic pressure or fluoroscopic/ultrasound confirmation of diaphragm paralysis or severe weakness with laterality; polysomnographic documentation of the SDB phenotype (REM-related hypoventilation versus obstructive events) with AHI and desaturation data; chronology linking the dysfunction to the sleep findings; exclusion of obesity-dominant obstructive sleep apnea and coexisting neuromuscular disease
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Coexisting neuromuscular disease (motor neuron disease, myopathy)
Phrenic neuropathy from cardiac or thoracic surgery as the independent driver

sourceReferences.citation: Steier J, Jolley CJ, Seymour J, Kaul S, Luo YM, Rafferty GF, Hart N, Polkey MI, Moxham J. Sleep-disordered breathing in unilateral diaphragm paralysis or severe weakness. Eur Respir J. 2008;32(6):1479-87. PMID 18684853.
sourceReferences.note: Instrumented PSG cohort (n=11 hemidiaphragm paralysis/severe weakness vs 11 matched controls): respiratory disturbance index 8.1 events/h in NREM and 26.0 events/h in REM sleep versus 0.4 and 0.7 in controls; diaphragm EMG drive doubled and increased further in REM; unilateral diaphragm dysfunction puts patients at risk of REM sleep-disordered breathing.

sourceReferences.citation: Khan A, Morgenthaler TI, Ramar K. Sleep disordered breathing in isolated unilateral and bilateral diaphragmatic dysfunction. J Clin Sleep Med. 2014;10(5):509-15. PMID 24910552.
sourceReferences.note: Retrospective Mayo cohort (n=66 referred for PSG): all patients with isolated diaphragmatic dysfunction had significant sleep-disordered breathing (mean AHI 26.6); CPAP controlled SDB in only 37.9%, with bilateral dysfunction 6.8 times more likely to fail CPAP - referred-population ascertainment and PAP-modality guards recorded.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 24910552; AHI in isolated diaphragmatic dysfunction and CPAP failure

sourceReferences.citation: Rock P, Rich PB. Postoperative pulmonary complications. Curr Opin Anaesthesiol. 2003;16(2):123-31. PMID 17021450.
sourceReferences.note: Perioperative review: inhibition of phrenic nerve output produces postoperative diaphragmatic dysfunction, and sleep-disordered breathing occurs after surgery even in patients without obstructive sleep apnea - supporting the ventilatory-pump pathway and the post-surgical context of acquired diaphragm dysfunction.
